summary: Extended reality (XR) is increasingly used in rehabilitation but its effectiveness in chronic respiratory conditions remains unclear. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental studies comparing XR-based interventions with usual care or alternatives. Searches were performed from inception to March 2025 and risk of bias was assessed by two independent reviewers. Fifteen experimental studies were included. XR-based interventions significantly improved 6-min walk distance (mean difference [MD] = 29.90 meters), forced vital capacity (MD = 0.37 liters), reduced dyspnea (standardized mean difference [SMD] = −0.61), anxiety (SMD = −2.08), and depression (SMD = −1.10), and improved quality of life (SMD = −1.87). No significant effects were observed for forced expiratory volume in one second percent predicted or fatigue. Subgroup analyses showed stronger effects in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and with comprehensive XR programs. Exercise-based XR improved quality of life only, while activities of daily living simulations improved forced expiratory volume in one second percent predicted, and nature-based interventions showed no significant benefit. Heterogeneity was substantial, but sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness of primary outcomes. XR-based rehabilitation may improve exercise capacity, symptoms, and quality of life, but larger multicenter trials are required to confirm long-term effectiveness and cost-effectiveness.
